Madam Vice-President, The security situation remains one of my main concerns. In several prefectures, including Umbommu, Vakaga, Waka, Umpende, Uam, and Nanambambere, civilians continue to be exposed to killings, kidnappings, sexual violence, looting, extortion and restrictions on freedom of movement. Transhumance-related violence and inter-community tensions also continue to bring loss of life and displacement. Between October 2025 and June 2026, Menosca's Human Rights Division documented 1,635 cases of human rights violations and abuses involving 2,804 victims. These figures are a reminder of the scale of the challenges that remain. Violations are attributed to different actors. I insist on a fundamental principle. All parties must respect international human rights law and international humanitarian law. And any credible allegations of violations of human rights and international humanitarian law must be promptly, independently and impartially investigated. Women and girls remain particularly vulnerable to conflict-related sexual violence and other forms of gender-based violence. Children also continue to face grave violations, including recruitment and use by armed groups, abductions, sexual violence, and attacks on schools and health facilities. I welcome the efforts made to release, care for, and reintegrate children associated with armed groups. These efforts must continue and must be strengthened. Madam Vice-President, developments since the end of the period covered by my report confirm both the progress made and the fragility of the situation. In early July, the situation in Am Dafok in Vakaga, once again demonstrated the risks to which the public in the border areas remains exposed. Over 16,000 people sought refuge with MONUSCO as a result of the violence. MONUSCO's intervention helped to save lives, maintain an administrative presence, and facilitate the delivery of humanitarian assistance. At the same time, there are encouraging signs. The disarmament and demobilization process is continuing. In August, 69 former UPC and anti-Balaka combatants voluntarily laid down their arms in Maloum in Waka province with the support of MONUSCO and the national authorities. And yet, forced displacement continues. At the beginning of September, over 250 people left the Ababogani area in Nana Mambere for Boua as a preventive measure. Constraints related to road conditions and bad weather continue to limit humanitarian access in certain areas. These developments show that peace in the Central African Republic is an ongoing process, not a definitive achievement. Excellencies, Justice and the fight against impunity must remain at the heart of this consolidation. I welcome the progress made by the Special Criminal Court and the efforts to reform the judicial system. However, difficulties remain. Prolonged pre-trial detention, slow procedures, weak enforcement of court decisions, and conditions of detention that remain in several institutions incompatible with international standards. Transitional justice must also move forward. Truth, justice, reparations, and guarantees of non-repetition are not secondary elements of the peace process. They are essential for the confidence of victims and the prevention of further violence. Madam Vice-President, Peace must also produce tangible results in the daily lives of Central Africans. Access to health, education, clean water, food and livelihoods remains severely inadequate in many regions. Over 2.8 million people are in need of humanitarian assistance and protection. Territorial inequalities remain deep. The strengthening of the state's authority must therefore go hand in hand with the deployment of public services and investments in rural areas. Another key issue is the future of the international presence, including MINUSCA. I fully recognize the importance of national ownership, but Any evolution in the mission's presence must be gradual, coordinated, and based on objective criteria in order to preserve the gains made in the areas of protection of civilians, security, humanitarian access, and institution building. This approach is in line with the concerns recently expressed by the African Union's Peace and Security Council, which stressed that any transition of MONUSCO must avoid the creation of a security vacuum. Vice President, I wish to conclude with a simple appeal. The Central African Republic now has an important opportunity to transform the gains of recent years into lasting peace. This requires continuing inclusive political dialogue, strengthening the rule of law, protecting civilians. fighting impunity, strengthening the participation of women and youth, protecting civic space, and investing in economic and social rights. I also call on the armed groups that have not yet done so to renounce violence, respect their peace commitments, and fully join the disarmament and reintegration process. Finally, I encourage international partners to maintain their political, technical and financial commitment to the Central African Republic. The progress made is real, as I have said, but it remains fragile. Lasting peace will only be possible if every Central African, wherever he or she lives, can benefit from security, justice, essential services and the effective protection of his for her rights. I thank you, Vice-President.
